claims.text: The initial Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy is in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution state.
Thermal exposure under service-like oxidizing conditions rapidly nucleates and grows intermetallic compounds.
The thermally induced intermetallic compounds form primarily along grain boundaries.
A distinct intermetallic precipitation threshold separates the two proposed heating regimes.
Intermetallic precipitation depletes or traps beneficial alloying elements that would otherwise contribute to protective surface oxides.
Mg contributes to the formation of stable, protective oxide films in the alloy.
Loss of protective oxide-film continuity increases susceptibility to corrosion and high-temperature oxidation.
Samples heated above the precipitation threshold will contain significantly more intermetallic phase than the initial state and samples heated below the threshold.
The increase in intermetallic content will coincide with reduced corrosion resistance.
The increase in intermetallic content will coincide with reduced high-temperature oxidation resistance.
The as-cast baseline has minimal intermetallic content.
The as-cast baseline exhibits established protective-oxide behavior.
Temperatures of 300–600 °C constitute the relevant service regime for the proposed alloy and degradation process.
High-temperature in-situ diffraction can track temperature-dependent phase transformations and oxide formation.
The kinetics of intermetallic nucleation and the quantitative effects on corrosion and oxidation resistance are unresolved.
